lead: Foot powder is a dusting powder applied to the feet and sometimes inside shoes and socks to absorb moisture, reduce odour and keep skin feeling dry. Formulations can be plain absorbents such as talc or starch, deodorant blends, or medicated powders containing antifungal agents. People use it as part of grooming and body-care routines so that feet look and smell cleaner and sandals, trainers and socks stay fresher through the day [6].

Foot odour is mainly caused by sweat, which creates a moist environment in which skin bacteria produce odorous compounds; Wikipedia lists daily washing, removing dead skin, clean cotton or wool socks, medicated insoles and foot powder among prevention measures [6]. Antifungal powders are also used for athlete's foot, where keeping feet dry is described as essential for preventing reinfection [10].

Evidence is mostly indirect. A 1974 report from a swimming bath found that supplying foot powder sachets to bathers coincided with a fall in tinea pedis incidence [2], and a skin-product study included a foot powder among four products tested for effects on the skin microbiome [1]. Contact allergy to an antimicrobial ingredient in one deodorant foot powder has been reported [3].

angle.text: A light dusting on clean, dry feet before socks is used to keep feet dry and fresh. Medicated versions are used for athlete's foot, where dryness is part of the management.

paras: Foot odour is generally attributed to sweat and bacterial breakdown of skin, and general references list foot hygiene, dry socks, medicated insoles and foot powder among prevention measures [6]. Powders are also used in the management of fungal infections of the feet; a podiatry review notes that infected shoes and socks can act as reservoirs for reinfection, so sanitising footwear is discussed alongside treatment [4]. A 1998 case report of 'toxic sock' syndrome describes a 17-year-old athlete with severe foot odour and itching who had tried an over-the-counter athlete's foot powder without result [9].

Wikipedia's foot odour article describes sweat as odourless in itself but a source of food and moisture for bacteria. Brevibacteria feed on dead skin and release a sulphur-like gas, while Staphylococcus epidermidis produces isovaleric acid, a compound also found in some strong-smelling cheeses. Closed shoes and synthetic socks that ventilate poorly can increase sweating and odour [6].

Prevention measures listed there include removing dead skin with a foot file, pumice or alpha hydroxy acid peel, washing daily with antibacterial soap, changing socks daily, choosing cotton or wool over synthetic fibres, and using medicated insoles and foot powder [6].

Wikipedia's athlete's foot article says prevention centres on keeping feet dry and limiting exposure to warm, damp places: breathable socks, sandals in gym showers, short toenails, and antifungal powder to help prevent recurrence. Without medication athlete's foot clears in roughly 30 to 40 percent of cases, while topical antifungals achieve much higher cure rates; treatment is applied as a cream, gel, spray or powder and typically continues two to six weeks after symptoms disappear. The condition affects about 15 percent of people globally and an estimated 70 percent will have it at some point [10].

Many dusting powders are made from talc, cornstarch or potato starch, sometimes with fragrance. Talcum powder was developed in the early 1890s by Frederick Barnett Kilmer of Johnson & Johnson, and Johnson's Baby Powder was in mass production by 1894 [11]. Foot-specific powders were developed alongside: a 1951 US Army medical bulletin describes a new foot powder to prevent cold injuries [7], and a 1960 podiatry paper reports clinical trials of a commercial oatmeal-based foot powder [5].
A 1975 case report described two people with allergic contact dermatitis to the antimicrobial Irgasan, one from a deodorant foot powder [3].

Wikipedia notes that inhaled talcum powder can cause aspiration pneumonia and granuloma, that cornstarch particles are larger and less likely to be inhaled, and that Johnson & Johnson stopped selling talc-based baby powder in the US and Canada in 2020 and moved to cornstarch, while maintaining that its talc contained no asbestos; litigation over talc has been brought in the US and UK [11]. Foot powders are applied to the feet rather than the genital area where those studies focused.

In a 1974 study of a public swimming pool, random samples of bathers were examined before and after individual foot powder sachets were provided; over three and a half years overall tinea pedis incidence fell from 8.5% to 2.1%, and in adult males from 21.5% to 6.9% [2]. The study was uncontrolled by modern standards. A 2019 study of 11 volunteers over nine weeks tested four products including a foot powder and examined skin chemistry and microbial diversity; its clearest reported change followed halting deodorant use [1]. A 1960 paper describes clinical trials of a commercial foot powder [5]. No trial specifically measuring cosmetic foot odour was found.

name: Foot powder

card.summary: Dusting powder for sweaty feet; sensible and cheap, but evidence is indirect.
card.note: Rare contact allergy to some deodorant ingredients reported.

quick.overview:
Foot powder is applied to feet or shoes to absorb moisture and reduce odour. Some products add antifungal or deodorant agents.

A 1974 swimming-bath report linked powder sachets to fewer athlete's foot cases, but no trial of cosmetic odour control was found.
quick.mechanism: Powders absorb sweat; odour is attributed to bacteria breaking down sweat and dead skin.
quick.risks: Contact allergy to an antimicrobial ingredient in one deodorant foot powder has been reported.
